questions.q: What does `docker exec -it catalog sh` actually do to the catalog container?
options: It replaces the container's main process with a shell, stopping the original application
It starts a new, second process (a shell) running alongside the container's existing main process
It restarts the container and clears its logs
It creates a brand new container named 'sh'
questions.explain: docker exec adds a new process inside an already-running container -- it does not replace or interrupt the main process, which is why exiting the shell doesn't stop the container.

questions.q: Why does exiting the shell from `docker exec -it catalog sh` not stop the catalog container?
options: Because docker exec containers are immune to the exit command
Because the shell was only a second process -- the container's main process (the Node server) keeps running independently
Because docker exec automatically restarts the container on exit
Because exit only closes the terminal window, not the shell
questions.explain: The container's lifecycle is tied to its main process, not to any exec'd process. The shell was additional; the server is still running.

questions.q: What does `docker cp` let you do?
options: Copy an entire running container to create an identical duplicate
Copy files between the host filesystem and a container's filesystem, in either direction, without needing a shell
Copy environment variables from one container to another
Clone a Docker image under a new tag
questions.explain: docker cp transfers files or directories between the host and a container's filesystem -- host to container or container to host -- without opening an interactive shell.

questions.q: In `docker stats` output showing `CPU % 84.2` and `MEM USAGE / LIMIT 412MiB / 512MiB`, what does this reading suggest?
options: The container is idle and using no resources
The container is close to its memory limit and under heavy CPU load -- a concrete lead for why it might be slow
The container has already crashed
The numbers only reflect disk usage, not CPU or memory
questions.explain: 412MiB used out of a 512MiB limit, combined with 84% CPU, points toward resource starvation as a likely cause of sluggish behavior -- a specific, actionable signal.

questions.q: In the suggested debugging pass (logs, stats, exec, inspect), why does `docker logs` come before `docker exec -it`?
options: Because docker exec requires the container to be stopped first
Because it moves from least invasive to most invasive -- checking existing output before opening an interactive session inside the container
Because docker logs is faster to type
There's no particular reason; the order doesn't matter
questions.explain: The suggested order starts with the least invasive check (reading existing logs) and only escalates to getting a shell inside the container if that doesn't reveal the problem.
